title: Hill Post — Ask why the shorter delivery cannot always be ridden
lead: Road lengths and stop heights are separate allowances in this puzzle. Count the road you ride and every upward change; these numbers are not bicycle-energy measurements.

questions.title: Is the shortest road always available?
questions.prompt: Choose Take the contour. Compare the ridge road with the road through Mill, Bridge and Orchard before riding.
questions.answer: The ridge costs four distance and four climbing. The longer road costs eight distance and one climbing. With a climbing allowance of one, the shortest route is not a usable route. The two limits cannot replace each other.

questions.title: Does the descent pay back the climb?
questions.prompt: Choose Two hills count twice. Follow the heights along the two-hill road without pressing a destination yet.
questions.answer: The road rises from zero to two, falls to zero, then rises to two again. Those upward changes add to four climbing, even though the finish is back at zero. A descent does not refund an earlier rise. The lower towpath fits the separate climbing allowance.

questions.title: Can a longer complete delivery need less climbing?
questions.prompt: Compare Deliver and bring back the reply with A gentler complete delivery. Include the ride home, not just the outward delivery.
questions.answer: The roof round trip uses eight distance and five climbing. The gentler round trip uses sixteen distance and three climbing. Returning over the roof adds a rise from the cafe’s height of three to the roof’s height of four. The price of going home belongs to the route too.

questions.title: Does reversing a loop remove a hill?
questions.prompt: Choose a complete journey with the same roads in either direction. Add only the upward height changes, including the ride home.
questions.answer: A closed circuit returns to its starting height, so its total rises equal its total falls. Reversing that identical circuit swaps rises and falls and keeps the same cumulative climbing. A different road can change the price; reversal alone cannot.

questions.title: Is a delivery finished at its last letter?
questions.prompt: On a journey whose goal is Post, pause after delivering the final letter. Read the next stop before choosing a road.
questions.answer: Not yet. The goal still requires the ride home. Delivered letters do not grant extra distance or climbing, and the allowance already spent stays spent. A route must pay for its whole stated journey.

questions.title: Does a taller stop imply a longer road?
questions.prompt: Compare a road length with the heights of its two endpoints before riding it.
questions.answer: They are separate authored quantities. Road length spends distance; a positive endpoint height difference spends climbing. Map spacing is a drawing aid, not the road-length formula. Neither allowance is a physical bicycle-energy estimate.
